newsitem.title: UK: MANCHESTER UNITED SOCCER SHARES LEAP ON BID TALK.
newsitem.headline: MANCHESTER UNITED SOCCER SHARES LEAP ON BID TALK.

text.p: Shares in British football league champions Manchester United jumped on Friday amid talk of a possible takeover bid for the club, traders said.
The shares spiked up to a record high of 500p before easing back to 471-1/2p but still up 19p.
Reports in the Times newspaper said a number of companies, including media and leisure group Granada Plc and brewer Whitbread Plc, had expressed a strong interest in buying United.
However, Whitbread told Reuters it was not true that it had expressed an interest in Manchester United, one of Britain's best known soccer clubs.
"It is not true that we have expressed an interest," said a spokeswoman for Whitbread.

"We would love to buy the club but there are as many beer drinkers in Liverpool, Newcastle and Chelsea," she said, adding that Whitbread would not want to do anything to upset customers who were fans of other clubs. "The report is complete rubbish."
A spokeswoman for Granada Plc said it could not comment, while Manchester United would not discuss the speculation.

The Times said a bid was likely to value United at more than 350 million pounds ($547.3 million). The club was said to have turned down a 300 million pound offer worth around 480 pence per share earlier this year from video and publishing group VCI Plc.
One attraction of the club to bidders is the opportunity afforded by pay-per-view television, which analysts say could dwarf income from even the current deal with satellite broadcaster BSkyB.

"You can come up with some very fancy numbers, given that they claim there are something like 200 million fans worldwide. You don't need to sell too much to too many to get some numbers which are very, very good indeed," said one industry analyst.

Last week, the club reported pre-tax profits of 15 million pounds, down from the previous year's 20 million pounds after falls in income from player transfers and a reduction in spectator capacity due to the rebuilding of its North stand.
Such figures are likely to pale in comparison to the money available from pay-per-view and whether the United board would accept a bid ahead of the potential bonanza is questionable.
"The numbers being chucked around about TV are very big and people shouldn't convince themselves that the big numbers aren't feasible: they are," said Vinay Bedi of brokers Wise Speke.
"They might not be quite as big as they think but we are certainly talking multiples of current revenues." ($1=.6395 Pound)
